items.stem: A colleague wants to paste a client's confidential memo into a public chatbot. What should they do first?

options.C: Keep it out unless policy and permission clearly allow it

options.A: Permission from the people or owners who control the data or work
options.B: A thumbs-up emoji from any coworker
options.C: The AI saying the text looks fine

items.stem: Why can AI output still raise copyright problems?

options.B: The output may copy protected wording or images from somewhere else
options.C: Copyright ends when text is digital

items.stem: Who usually stays responsible when AI-assisted text goes to a client?

options.B: Nobody, if the AI wrote most of it
options.C: The person and organization who send the work

items.stem: A designer feeds a rival's poster into an AI and publishes a near copy. Main issue?

options.A: They used someone else's protected work without rights
options.C: The file name was too long

items.stem: Your firm buys a research PDF marked "internal use only." Safe AI move?

options.A: Upload it to any free tool to summarize for social media
options.B: Follow the license and company rules before any AI use or sharing
options.C: Share it widely so the AI can "learn faster"

items.stem: Open public facts differ from a full news article because:

options.A: All text online is free to copy forever
options.B: Short facts may be usable, but the article's wording can still be protected

items.stem: Before you put customer data into any AI tool, you should know:

options.A: Whether you have the right and the consent to use that data that way
options.C: Only whether the summary sounds polite

items.stem: An AI writes a poem "in the style of" a living author and you sell it. Best reading?

options.A: Style mimicry always erases every duty
options.B: Selling it can still step on rights and trust — check rules before you publish
